before: A meta element with name="description" gives a short description of the document through content. It is not an ordinary visible paragraph. Search services may use it, replace it or ignore it; writing it does not guarantee a particular search snippet or ranking.

A link with rel="icon" names an icon resource. href gives its location, while type can state its media type. The file must exist, and each browser chooses how and where to display it. This differs from an a link with clickable words in the body.

These fragments belong inside head, beside the existing title and charset metadata.

```html
<meta name="description" content="Short observations from a neighborhood tree survey.">
<link rel="icon" href="tree-mark.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
```

The description is stored in content. The icon link points to tree-mark.svg; it does not contain the picture. Use your own asset or one whose license permits your use, retaining required notices.

Give Cloud notebook the supplied short description and a link to cloud-mark.svg. Keep its title and visible h1 separate. The exercise checks metadata structure; it does not contact search engines or prove icon rendering. The companion icon is original markup supplied with this lesson.
after:
A page description is a short summary stored in the HTML. It does not appear as a paragraph on the page.

```html
<meta name="description" content="Short observations from a neighborhood tree survey.">
```

`name="description"` tells us what this information is. `content` holds the summary. A search service may show this summary, but it can choose different words.

A page icon is a small picture a browser may show beside the page title.

```html
<link rel="icon" href="tree-mark.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
```

`rel="icon"` says what the file is for. `href` gives its location. `type` says it is an SVG picture. The file must exist; this tag does not draw the picture.
On a full HTML page, put the description and icon link inside `<head>`, with `<title>`. Keep the visible `<h1>` inside `<body>`. This exercise uses a small piece of HTML to practise the new tags.

Keep the starter title and heading. Add a description with the exact text `A small record of cloud shapes seen from one garden.` Add an icon link to `cloud-mark.svg`, which is included with the lesson. To see the icon on a downloaded page, use a full page with these tags in `<head>` and keep the icon file beside it.

before.question: A search service shows different wording from your meta description. Does that alone mean your HTML description failed to parse?
choices: No. The service can choose its own snippet.
Yes. Search results must reproduce content exactly.
Yes. meta descriptions are visible headings.
before.explanation: The description supplies metadata, not a command that every external service must display verbatim.

after.question: A search result shows different words from your page description. Is the HTML necessarily wrong?
choices: No. A search service can choose its own summary.
Yes. It must show the exact description.
Yes. The description must be a visible heading.
after.explanation: The description offers a summary. It does not control what every search service shows.
